sections.body: This field is about making quantitative research repeatable and checkable, and using AI to help with the mechanics of data work. AI is currently doing things like generating notebook cells, converting plain language questions into database queries, suggesting statistical tests, and simulating data before a study runs. It is not doing the thinking for the researcher, but it is reducing the time spent on boilerplate code and setup. The work here is practical: notebooks that rerun without manual fixes, code that passes basic statistical checks, and designs that can be stress-tested on synthetic data. The site's library of 135 research papers and 805 scientific models reflects the scale of material this section draws from, but the section itself focuses on the day-to-day tools.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The state of this work is uneven. Reproducible notebooks are common, but true one-click reproduction across different machines and data versions is still rare. Plain language querying works well for simple questions and small schemas, but it degrades when the data model is complex or the question is ambiguous. Large-scale compute on institutional data is feasible with AI help for orchestration, but security and governance remain hard limits, not solved problems. Statistical code generation is reliable for standard analyses, yet it can silently produce wrong results when assumptions are violated. Testing a study design before data collection is promising, but the simulations are only as good as the assumptions fed into them, and many researchers still treat them as a formality rather than a real check.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to make their own work rerunnable would start with Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines, which covers the practical setup of environments and versioning. If the goal is to explore a dataset without writing SQL or Python, Asking Data Questions in Plain Language shows what current tools can and cannot translate. Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data is for those working with sensitive or very large datasets, where the bottleneck is not code but access and infrastructure. Writing Statistical Code with AI addresses the specific risk of generated analysis scripts, including how to check them. Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection is the earliest stage in the workflow, useful for a researcher who wants to catch design flaws before spending money or time on real data. Together these pages move from preparation to execution to validation, but each can be read on its own.
